replacement: Father Iosif walked away, grieved all the more because he had put his opinion forward so timidly, as if he hardly believed it himself. He could see, to his distress, that something very unseemly was beginning, and that there were positive signs of disobedience. Little by little, all the sensible monks were reduced to silence, as Father Iosif had been. The result was that everyone who loved the elder and had accepted the eldership with devout obedience was all at once terribly cast down, and exchanged timid glances when they met. The enemies of elders, who saw the institution as a novelty, now carried their heads proudly. “The late elder Varsonofy gave off no smell of corruption, but a sweet fragrance,” they recalled with spite. “But he earned that glory not as an elder, but as a holy man.”
“Have you, too, fallen into temptation?” cried Father Païssy. “Can you be with those of little faith?” he added sadly.

Father Païssy was right, of course, to decide that his “dear boy” would come back. He may even have seen, to some degree, what Alyosha’s spiritual state really meant. Still, I have to admit that I would find it very hard to give a clear account of that strange, hazy time in the life of the young hero I love so much. Father Païssy asked sadly, “Are you too with those of little faith?” I could answer confidently for Alyosha, “No, he is not with those of little faith. Quite the opposite.” All his trouble, in fact, came from having great faith. But the trouble was there just the same, and it hurt so badly that even long afterwards Alyosha remembered that sorrowful day as one of the bitterest and most fatal of his life. Suppose someone asks: “Could all his grief and turmoil have come only from the fact that his elder’s body showed signs of early decay, instead of working miracles at once?” I have to answer without beating about the bush, “Yes, it certainly was.” I only ask the reader not to hurry to laugh at my young hero’s pure heart. I have no wish to apologize for him, or to excuse his innocent faith by pointing to his youth, or how little he had studied, or any such thing. On the contrary, I declare that I truly respect the qualities of his heart. A youth who took in impressions cautiously, whose love was lukewarm, and whose mind was too prudent for his age and therefore worth little, might well, I admit, have escaped what happened to my hero. But sometimes it does a man more credit to be swept away by a feeling, however unreasonable, that grows out of great love, than to remain unmoved. This is even truer in youth, because a young man who is always sensible is not to be trusted and is worth little—that’s my opinion!
“Well, well! You surprise me, brother!” Rakitin stared at him in amazement. “Anyway, vodka or sausage, this is a first-rate chance and we mustn’t miss it. Come on.”
